claims.claim: Social organization refers to the patterned, stable ways people arrange themselves into groups; Britannica describes social structure as a distinct and stable arrangement of institutions with patterned social relationships, and OpenStax treats hierarchy as a type of social organization.

An age set is a formally organized group of people of roughly the same age who share a common social status with permitted roles and responsibilities; the stages such groups pass through are called age grades.

An egalitarian society is one in which the diverse roles in a group are given the same decision-making power and accorded the same respect; in such societies power is often afforded by age grades, with elders holding the most influence.

Social stratification is the division of society into groups ranked according to wealth, power, or prestige, and it can be based on racial category, socioeconomic status, kinship, religion, birth order, or gender.
A class is a group of people with the same socioeconomic status and proximity to power, most often associated with the capitalist mode of production.

Secret societies are membership organizations marked by restricted knowledge, initiation ceremonies, and secrecy; many have been formed primarily for social, benevolent, charitable, and educational purposes.
Sociality is the term anthropologists use for how people construct and maintain their personal and group relations, including through chosen, voluntary connections.

Elman Service (1962) proposed four main forms of social organization — band, tribe, chiefdom, and state — linked to subsistence patterns; the typology is a historical attribution, and many anthropologists now avoid the word 'tribe'.
Egalitarian societies are organized, not structureless: decision-making runs through discussion, consensus, and age grades, and influence is persuasive rather than coercive.
Social organization serves functions including coordination of collective activity, the production of group identity, and the allocation of resources among members.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are egalitarian societies 'unstructured'? Popular accounts sometimes treat societies without formal leadership as having no social organization at all.
positions: OpenStax 8.2: band societies are strongly egalitarian yet make decisions through discussion and consensus, with no formal positions of leadership — organization without offices.
OpenStax 9.1: in egalitarian societies power is usually afforded by age grades, with elders holding the most power — hierarchy of influence without coercive enforcement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that egalitarian means equal decision-making power and respect among roles, not the absence of organization; consensus itself is a structure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Definitional nuance on age sets: is membership gendered and is the 'age grade' a stage or the whole system?
positions: OpenStax 8.2/8-key-terms: age sets are groups of people of roughly the same age, most often gendered, with a distinctive role in society; the age grade is the level in the hierarchy.
Britannica age-set: an age set is a formally organized group of every male (or female) of comparable age; each stage of life is known as an age grade.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources agree: the set is the group of same-aged people, the grade is the stage or level; the lesson presents the two terms with that distinction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Use of the word 'tribe' as a category of social organization.
positions: Service's historical typology (band, tribe, chiefdom, state) is still taught as intellectual history.
OpenStax cautions that many anthropologists now avoid 'tribe' because of connotations of primitivism and groupthink.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the typology to Service as history and avoids 'tribe' as a live descriptive category, per the source's caution.

sourceRecords.title: 8.2 Acephalous Societies: Bands and Tribes — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220930222131 of the canonical URL (openstax.org now serves a JS shell; capture contains full text). Supports: age sets as groups of similarly aged people with common status, roles, and responsibilities; age grades as levels in the hierarchy; gendered age sets; lifelong bonds crossing lineage and clan lines; the Shavante (Xavante) example; egalitarian band societies, consensus decision-making, and persuasive power. Facts synthesized into original prose; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 8.1 Colonialism and the Categorization of Political Systems — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20221002071207 of the canonical URL. sourceRecords.title: Chapter 8 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220924024342 of the canonical URL. Supports definitions: age sets ('gendered groups of people of roughly the same age who play a distinctive role in society with important social obligations and abilities'), social stratification ('the division of society into groups that are ranked according to wealth, power, or prestige'), and the asafo example of a non-kin association in Akan societies.

sourceRecords.title: 9.1 Theories of Inequity and Inequality — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220924024340 of the canonical URL. Supports: hierarchy defined as a type of social organization in which certain people or roles are given more power and prestige; the egalitarian definition (diverse roles given the same decision-making power and respect; power usually afforded by age grades with elders holding the most power); social stratification as the hierarchical organization of groups based on racial category, socioeconomic status, kinship, religion, birth order, or gender; functionalist view of egalitarian versus stratified societies.

sourceRecords.title: Chapter 9 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220929152211 of the canonical URL. Supports definitions: egalitarian, hierarchy ('a type of social organization in which certain people or roles are given more power and prestige than others'), class ('a group of people with the same socioeconomic status and proximity to power'), and caste.

sourceRecords.title: 9.2 Systems of Inequality — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20221005152132 of the canonical URL. Supports the class principle: in a class-based system status stems from wealth and proximity to power, most often associated with the capitalist mode of production; Weber's three components (socioeconomic status, prestige, political party) and Bourdieu's capitals are noted as background. Used factually, without policy positions.

sourceRecords.title: 15.8 Digital Media, New Socialities — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax, Rice University)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220930053140 of the canonical URL. Supports the definition of sociality — how people construct and maintain their personal and group relations — used for the voluntary-groups section and the functions of social organization.

sourceRecords.title: Age Set | Sociology, Anthropology & Culture — Encyclopaedia Britannica
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20251009123855 of the canonical URL. Supports: an age set as a formally organized group of every male (or female) of comparable age; membership passes through named stages each with a distinctive status and role, each stage known as an age grade; Nuer example (sets formed at roughly ten-year intervals by initiation, equality within a set, deference between junior and senior sets). Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Secret Society — Encyclopaedia Britannica
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20260528022802 of the canonical URL. Supports: secret societies as membership organizations with restricted knowledge, initiation ceremonies, and common structure and function; many modern secret societies were formed primarily for social and benevolent purposes, charitable and educational programs, and served as principal means of social and civic activity in many communities. Used for the one-line factual description; no value judgments.

sourceRecords.title: Social Structure | Definition, Examples, Theories, & Facts — Encyclopaedia Britannica (José Itzigsohn)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20260810180157 of the canonical URL. Supports the working definition: social structure refers to the distinct and stable arrangement of institutions through which individuals in a society interact and live together, focusing on patterned social relationships. Combined with OpenStax's 'hierarchy as a type of social organization' to ground the lesson's working definition of social organization as the patterned ways people arrange themselves into groups.
